title: The Kalamas ask
hook: a town tired of teachers asks the Buddha whom to believe; he ends with four comforts that hold whether or not there is a next life (AN 3.65)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Yasa's night: a rich young man walked out of a party at three in the morning, and found someone waiting on the road.
screen: `YASA'S NIGHT — WALK OUT OF THE PARTY.`

segments.voice: Yasa's friends come, then fifty more, and soon the Buddha sends them all walking, for the good of the many. The roads of India are full of walking teachers. In a town called Kesaputta, the people, the Kalamas, have had enough. Teacher after teacher comes through, praises his own teaching, and runs down everyone else's. Then the next one does the same. And when the Buddha arrives, they put it to him plainly: we don't know who to believe. Even about whether there's another life at all.
screen: `SENT WALKING, FOR THE GOOD OF THE MANY.` → `TEACHER AFTER TEACHER.` → `WHO DO WE BELIEVE?`

segments.voice: The Buddha's first answer surprises them. Your doubt is reasonable, he says. You're right to be unsure. He goes on to give them a way to test any teaching, and we'll come back to that later on the path. Today is about the way the talk ends, the part people often skip. He describes someone whose mind is free of hatred and ill will, clear and clean. That person, he says, has four comforts, right here in this life. If there is another world, and good and bad deeds bear fruit, then I'll arise somewhere good. If there isn't, then here and now I live free of hostility, at ease. If harm comes to those who do harm, I intend harm to no one, so how could it touch me? And if it doesn't, I'm clean either way. The Pali word is assasa: comfort, the kind that lets you breathe out. Notice what he doesn't say. He doesn't tell the Kalamas to settle the question of rebirth before they begin. Rebirth runs all through his teaching, and many Buddhists hold it close. But this talk starts with what anyone can see. Teachers read it in more than one way. Some say the Buddha is meeting doubters where they are, before he teaches more. Others take it as a welcome to begin with the question still open. Either way, the Kalamas walk away with something they can use tomorrow morning. And if you're not sure about rebirth yet, you're in company the Buddha himself sat down with.
screen: `YOUR DOUBT IS REASONABLE.` · `IF THERE IS ANOTHER LIFE, IT GOES WELL.` · `IF THERE ISN'T, THIS ONE ALREADY DOES.` · `BEGIN WITH THE QUESTION OPEN.` · then, large: `GOOD EITHER WAY.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one big question you can't settle, about what comes after or anything else, and don't try to answer it; picture setting it down beside you, still there, still open. Then notice what is true without the answer: the breath coming in, the breath going out, and the chance, today, to act without ill will.
Assasa. Comfort, relief, a breath let out: the four comforts the Buddha gave the Kalamas, which hold whether or not there is another life.
Your line: good either way. A life without ill will is good whether or not there's another one. Day sixty-six, done.

howItsDone: Teachers often quote the Kalama Sutta to newcomers who are unsure about rebirth; many Buddhist communities welcome people to practice while the question is still open.

fork.setup: you're one of the Kalamas. teacher after teacher says only he is right. one more arrives. what do you do?
options: ignore him; they're all the same.
ask him how to tell who's telling the truth.
fork.reveal: the Kalamas asked the Buddha exactly that, and he began by telling them their doubt was reasonable.

original.note: Pali assasa: comfort, relief; the same word can mean breathing in, a breath of ease.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Kalama Sutta says believe whatever feels right.
what it means: test a teaching by what it does, and live so that your life is good whether or not there is a next one.
what a scholar hears: AN 3.65 (Kesamutti, the Kalama Sutta): its often-quoted list of what not to rely on comes first; the four assasa, the comforts, close it, and are quoted far less.

chat.says: Do I have to believe in rebirth before I can start practicing?
options: Not to start. He told the Kalamas a life without ill will is good either way.
Yes. He told the Kalamas to settle that question before anything else.
No. He told the Kalamas rebirth is just a story they could ignore.
chat.meaning: His four comforts hold whether or not there's another life. He didn't ask the Kalamas to settle rebirth first, though it runs through his teaching.

Kalamas.meaning: the people of Kesaputta, who asked whom to believe

notes: Rewritten 2026-10-06 from the five-year map; confirm with the Keeper.
Replaces 'Sixty sent out' (carika). The send-out is kept in the hook's first line; the sixty and 'for the good of the many' also appear on days 67, 147 and 1029–1030.

Why: 'do I have to believe in rebirth?' is the loudest worry in the research (map need 1). This is the early, light answer; the Kalama list of what not to rely on stays on day 321 (which now points back here), ehipassiko on day 325, and the deep rebirth teaching in year 2 (339–341, 452, 460).
Sensitive (rebirth): the script says rebirth runs through the teaching and many hold it close, and gives two readings of the sutta without choosing. Confirm the framing.
Confirm: the four assurances paraphrased from AN 3.65; the spelling assasa/assāsa and the 'breathing' sense in the original game.
Chronology: the Kalama visit is not dated in the texts; placed in the 'teaching spreads' week without claiming when it happened.
